summary: Describes how an EPP session is carried over a single TCP connection. It requires TLS to protect the information exchanged between EPP client and server. It was replaced by RFC 4934.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains how the registry language travels over an internet connection, and it insists the connection be sealed so no one can read it.

questions: how to connect to domain registry
subtitle: Carrying domain registry messages over TCP with security.

tldr.problem: The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) needed a standard way to be transmitted between domain registries and registrars over reliable internet connections.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3734 maps EPP messages onto TCP connections protected by TLS to provide secure, reliable transport. Messages are framed with a 32-bit length field preceding the XML payload.
tldr.outcome: EPP TCP transport became the standard for domain registry communication. RFC 4934 superseded this specification in 2007 with refinements.

today: RFC 3734 is obsoleted by RFC 4934, which was published in 2007 with clarifications and updates to the EPP TCP transport mapping.

sections.title: Introduction to EPP over TCP
sections.content:
EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) is a framework for provisioning objects, such as domain names, within the Domain Name System. This RFC describes how to carry EPP messages over a TCP connection protected by TLS (Transport Layer Security).

A registrar client connects to a registry server on a TCP port, typically port 700. After the TCP connection is established, both sides perform a TLS handshake to authenticate each other and establish encrypted communication. Only after successful TLS authentication does the server send an EPP greeting, and the client may then send EPP commands.
sections.plainLanguage: A registrar is like a postal clerk; a registry is like the post office. The clerk needs a secure, locked phone line to the post office to send commands like "register this domain name."

sections.title: Session Management
sections.content:
The EPP session is mapped directly onto the TCP connection. The client initiates a TCP connection to the server, which listens on a configured TCP port. After the connection is established and TLS handshake completes, the server sends an EPP greeting message.

The client can then send EPP commands. An EPP session normally ends when the client sends a logout command, which causes the server to close the TCP connection. A server may also timeout inactive sessions or impose limits on how long an EPP session may remain open. If a server receives and processes a command but the connection closes before the response is sent, the server may attempt to undo the command to maintain consistency.
sections.plainLanguage: One EPP session uses one phone call. When the call ends, the session ends. The registry server can hang up if nobody is talking for too long.

sections.title: Sending Commands and Responses
sections.content:
Except for the server greeting, all EPP messages are initiated by the client as commands. The server returns a response to each command on the same TCP connection. A client may send multiple commands before receiving responses to previous ones (command pipelining), though the server should not require this.

Each EPP command is processed independently and in the order sent. Commands are idempotent, meaning that processing a command more than once produces the same net effect on the registry as processing it once. A server may limit the time a client has to send a well-formed command and may close the connection if this limit is exceeded.
sections.plainLanguage: The registrar asks a question; the registry answers. The registrar can ask more questions without waiting for all answers, like leaving multiple voicemails. Each question always gets the same answer, no matter how many times you ask.

sections.title: Data Unit Format
sections.content:
Each EPP data unit transported by TCP consists of two parts: a 32-bit header field describing the total length of the data unit (measured in octets in network byte order), followed by the EPP XML instance. The length field includes itself in the total count, so the minimum value is 4 bytes (the header alone).

This framing allows the TCP receiver to know exactly how many octets comprise each EPP message, even though TCP itself does not preserve message boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending each command, write down how many bytes are about to arrive, like labeling a package with its weight. This helps the other side know when a message ends.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
EPP alone provides only weak authentication: a username and password in plain text. The TLS layer MUST protect EPP sessions against eavesdropping, tampering, and command forgery. Both the client and server must authenticate each other using the TLS Handshake Protocol. Signatures on the complete certificate chains for both machines MUST be validated, including verifying certificate validity periods and machine names.

EPP service MUST NOT be granted until after a successful TLS handshake and certificate validation. EPP uses an additional user identifier and password (beyond the machine authentication from TLS) to identify the specific user. Servers should protect against TCP denial of service attacks using firewall filters and other defenses.
sections.plainLanguage: The locked line is the TLS connection. Both sides show ID cards (certificates) and check them before talking. Even with a locked line, the registrar still sends a username and password to prove who they are.
